8ea289b803:
Expected lesion: granulomatous inflammation with caseating granulomas: secondary (reactivation) pulmonary tuberculosis.

Gross

  • Apical or posterior upper-lobe lesion with a cavity lined by yellow-grey, cheesy (caseous) material.
  • Surrounding consolidation, fibrosis and pleural thickening; satellite lesions may spread through the bronchi.

Microscopy

  • Central caseous necrosis: structureless, granular, pink debris (cell outlines lost).
  • Surrounded by epithelioid macrophages (abundant pale cytoplasm, slipper-shaped nuclei).
  • Langhans giant cells with nuclei arranged in a horseshoe at the periphery.
  • A cuff of lymphocytes, then fibroblasts and fibrosis at the edge.
  • Acid-fast bacilli shown with the Ziehl-Neelsen stain.
18f95366e2:
Whether ischaemia ends as an infarct, and how large it is, depends on:

  • Nature of the blood supply: organs with a dual or collateral supply (lung, liver, hand) resist infarction; end-arterial organs (kidney, spleen) infarct readily.
  • Rate of occlusion: slow narrowing allows collaterals to develop; sudden occlusion does not.
  • Vulnerability of the tissue to hypoxia: neurons die after 3 to 4 minutes and myocardium after 20 to 30 minutes, while fibroblasts survive much longer.
  • Oxygen content of the blood: anaemia, hypoxaemia or heart failure make infarction more likely and larger.
add07c611d:
Provisional diagnosis: septic shock (sepsis with hypotension and multi-organ dysfunction).

Investigations

  • Blood culture (before antibiotics) and culture of the likely source: urine, sputum, wound or CSF.
  • Complete blood count: leukocytosis or leukopenia, thrombocytopenia.
  • Serum lactate (tissue hypoperfusion), CRP and procalcitonin.
  • Coagulation profile: PT, APTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer (for DIC).
  • Organ function: urea, creatinine and electrolytes, liver function tests, blood glucose, arterial blood gases.
  • Imaging for the source: chest X-ray, ultrasound of the abdomen.
6faddc8cc2:
Most likely diagnosis: septic shock.

Pathogenesis

  • Recognition of microbes: bacterial products (such as endotoxin) bind Toll-like and other receptors on macrophages, neutrophils and endothelium.
  • Cytokine storm: TNF, IL-1 and IL-6 drive fever and a systemic inflammatory response; complement is activated.
  • Vasodilation: nitric oxide and prostaglandins dilate vessels, so blood pressure falls.
  • Endothelial injury: leaky vessels cause oedema and loss of circulating volume.
  • Procoagulant state: tissue factor is expressed, so microthrombi form and DIC can follow.
  • Metabolic changes: insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia, later adrenal insufficiency.
  • Multi-organ failure: hypoperfusion and microthrombi injure the lungs (ARDS), kidneys, liver and brain (loss of consciousness).
b56c2198f5:
Salient features of autosomal dominant disorders

  • A single mutant allele is enough to cause disease.
  • Both sexes are affected with equal frequency, and either parent can pass it on.
  • Vertical transmission: the disease appears in every generation.
  • Each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk.
  • Incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity are common.
  • Many cases arise from a new mutation, especially when the disease reduces fertility.
  • Onset is often delayed to adulthood; the mutant genes often code for structural proteins or receptors.
  • Examples: Marfan syndrome, familial hypercholesterolaemia, adult polycystic kidney disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, Huntington disease, hereditary spherocytosis, familial adenomatous polyposis.

Turner syndrome

  • Karyotype: 45,X (complete loss of one X) in most cases; the rest are mosaics or have a structurally abnormal X.
  • Features: short stature, webbed neck, low posterior hairline, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus and lymphoedema of hands and feet at birth.
  • Heart and kidney: coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, horseshoe kidney.
  • Gonads: streak ovaries, causing primary amenorrhoea, infertility and absent secondary sexual characteristics.
  • Intelligence is usually normal; hypothyroidism is common.
  • Diagnosis: karyotyping; buccal smear shows no Barr body.
1b4d379840:
• Dysplasia: disordered growth with loss of uniformity and orientation of cells: pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio and mitoses above the basal layer. Example: cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, dysplasia in Barrett oesophagus.
  • Carcinoma in situ: dysplastic change through the whole epithelial thickness while the basement membrane remains unbreached, so spread has not yet begun. Example: CIN III (HSIL) of the cervix, ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast.
  • Grading: how differentiated the tumour cells are and how many mitoses they show (well, moderately or poorly differentiated). Examples: Gleason score in prostate cancer, Nottingham grade in breast cancer.
  • Staging: how far the tumour has spread, by the TNM system: size and local extent of the primary (T), lymph node spread (N) and distant metastasis (M). Example: breast carcinoma T2 N1 M0. Stage predicts outcome better than grade.
e5babc0b5f:
Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E and K.

Functions of vitamin D

  • Increases intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.
  • Keeps serum calcium and phosphate high enough for mineralisation of bone (osteoid).
  • With PTH, mobilises calcium from bone by stimulating osteoclast formation (through RANKL) when serum calcium falls.
  • Increases renal tubular reabsorption of calcium.
  • Other roles: suppresses PTH secretion and modulates immunity.
2360cd3649:
Risk factors of IHD

  • Not modifiable: increasing age, male sex, family history and genetic factors.
  • Modifiable: hypertension, smoking, diabetes mellitus, raised LDL or low HDL cholesterol, obesity and the metabolic syndrome, physical inactivity.
  • Others: raised CRP, lipoprotein(a), hyperhomocysteinaemia.

Cardiac markers raised in MI

  • Cardiac troponin I and T: most sensitive and specific; rise in 2 to 4 hours, stay raised for 7 to 10 days.
  • CK-MB: begins to climb within a few hours, is highest around the first day and is back to baseline by day three, which makes it useful for spotting a second infarct.
  • Myoglobin: rises earliest but is not specific to the heart.
26d96db264:
(a) Probable diagnosis: stable angina pectoris, chest pain on exertion relieved by rest, from coronary atherosclerosis (risk factors: smoking, heavy exertion, family history of sudden cardiac death).

(b) Outcomes if untreated

  • Progression to unstable angina.
  • Acute myocardial infarction.
  • Sudden cardiac death, usually from an arrhythmia.
  • Chronic ischaemic heart disease with progressive heart failure.
  • Arrhythmias.
829322b3dc:
(a) Most likely diagnosis: acute myocardial infarction.

(b) Pathogenesis

  • An atherosclerotic plaque (risk raised by hypertension and diabetes) ruptures or erodes, exposing collagen and the lipid core.
  • Platelets adhere, aggregate and release thromboxane A2, ADP and serotonin, which also cause vasospasm.
  • Tissue factor activates coagulation, and within minutes a thrombus occludes the coronary artery.
  • Ischaemia stops aerobic metabolism: contractility is lost within a minute, and cell injury becomes irreversible after 20 to 40 minutes.
  • Necrosis spreads from the subendocardium outwards as a wavefront and becomes transmural over 3 to 6 hours.

(c) Cardiac biomarkers

  • Troponin I and T (most specific), CK-MB (helps detect re-infarction) and myoglobin (early, not specific).
4e7d325838:
The revised Jones criteria (American Heart Association, 2015) diagnose rheumatic fever.

  • Essential: proof of recent group A streptococcal infection, such as a high or climbing ASO titre, a positive throat swab culture or a positive rapid antigen test.
  • First attack: 2 major criteria, or 1 major and 2 minor.
  • Recurrence: 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, or 3 minor.

Major criteria

  • Carditis (clinical, or subclinical on echocardiography).
  • Arthritis: polyarthritis (in moderate or high-risk populations, monoarthritis or polyarthralgia also count).
  • Sydenham chorea.
  • Erythema marginatum.
  • Subcutaneous nodules.

Minor criteria

  • Polyarthralgia (monoarthralgia in high-risk populations).
  • Fever (38.5 °C, or 38 °C in high-risk populations).
  • Raised ESR (60 mm in the first hour, or 30 in high-risk populations) or CRP (3 mg/dL or more).
  • Prolonged PR interval, unless carditis is already counted.
fe1786461f:
Infective endocarditis: microbial infection of the heart valves or endocardium, usually bacterial, forming bulky, friable vegetations of thrombus and organisms.

Predisposing factors

  • Rheumatic heart disease.
  • Congenital heart disease: VSD, PDA, bicuspid aortic valve.
  • Mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation; degenerative calcific valve disease.
  • Prosthetic valves; previous endocarditis.
  • Intravenous drug use (often the tricuspid valve); indwelling catheters.
  • Dental procedures and poor oral hygiene; diabetes and immunosuppression.

Complications

  • Cardiac: valve destruction and regurgitation, heart failure, ring abscess, conduction block.
  • Embolic: septic infarcts in the brain, kidney and spleen; mycotic aneurysms.
  • Renal: immune complex glomerulonephritis, infarcts.
  • Systemic: septicaemia; Osler nodes, Janeway lesions and Roth spots.
b938722278:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: acute rheumatic fever after untreated streptococcal pharyngitis (migratory polyarthritis, carditis, raised ASO titre).

(ii) Characteristic cardiac lesion: the Aschoff body, a focus of fibrinoid change surrounded by lymphocytes and Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells, seen in a pancarditis. Small warty vegetations form along the lines of valve closure, and long-term damage leads to chronic rheumatic valve disease, most often mitral stenosis.
b8ac8dfff1:
(a) Comment: the picture suggests tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease), tuberculosis of the spine with constitutional symptoms (evening fever, night sweats, weight loss) in a person from a high-risk background.

(b) Special stain: the Ziehl-Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli (auramine-rhodamine fluorescent stain is an alternative). The biopsy also shows caseating granulomas.
1bb746143b:
Probable diagnosis: pulmonary tuberculosis.

Investigations

  • Sputum for acid-fast bacilli (Ziehl-Neelsen stain), two to three samples.
  • GeneXpert MTB/RIF: detects M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance within hours.
  • Sputum culture (Lowenstein-Jensen or liquid culture) with drug sensitivity.
  • Chest X-ray: upper-zone infiltrates or cavities.
  • Complete blood count and ESR (raised ESR, lymphocytosis).
  • Supportive tests: Mantoux (tuberculin) test or an IGRA blood test, and screening for HIV.
66e71fab83:
Tuberculosis is a disease of cell-mediated immunity (type IV hypersensitivity).

  • Entry: inhaled droplet nuclei reach the alveoli and are taken up by macrophages.
  • Early unchecked growth: the bacilli block phagolysosome maturation and multiply for about 3 weeks, spreading through lymphatics and blood (seeding other organs).
  • TH1 response: macrophages present antigen and secrete IL-12, so TH1 cells develop and release interferon-gamma.
  • Macrophage activation: interferon-gamma lets macrophages destroy the bacilli (phagolysosome maturation, nitric oxide, reactive oxygen species).
  • Granuloma formation: TNF recruits monocytes, which become epithelioid cells and giant cells; the centre undergoes caseous necrosis. The tuberculin test becomes positive.
  • Primary TB: Ghon focus plus hilar nodes (Ghon complex), usually healing by fibrosis and calcification.
  • Secondary TB: reactivation or reinfection in a sensitised host, giving apical cavitation.
  • Poor immunity (HIV, malnutrition) allows progressive and miliary disease.
fb6abfcc08:
• Hypercalcaemia: PTH-related peptide, mainly from squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Cushing syndrome: ACTH, from small cell carcinoma.
  • SIADH with hyponatraemia: ADH, from small cell carcinoma.
  • Neuromuscular syndromes: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (antibodies to calcium channels), cerebellar degeneration and sensory neuropathy, mostly with small cell carcinoma.
  • Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy and clubbing, especially with adenocarcinoma.
  • Hypercoagulability: migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome), DIC.
  • Others: carcinoid syndrome, gynaecomastia (hCG), acanthosis nigricans, dermatomyositis.
db153e2251:
Etiopathogenesis

  • Cigarette smoking: the main cause, related to pack-years. Carcinogens such as polycyclic hydrocarbons and nitrosamines form DNA adducts and cause mutations (TP53, KRAS).
  • Occupational and environmental: asbestos, radon and uranium, arsenic, chromium, nickel, air pollution.
  • Molecular: EGFR mutations and ALK rearrangements, especially in adenocarcinoma of non-smokers.
  • Stepwise change (squamous type): hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, then invasive carcinoma.

Four common carcinomas

  • Adenocarcinoma.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Small cell carcinoma.
  • Large cell carcinoma.
861ad7525b:
(a) Most likely type: squamous cell carcinoma, a central (hilar) tumour strongly linked to smoking. Small cell carcinoma is also central and should be considered.

How to proceed

  • Imaging: chest X-ray, then contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen for the tumour and staging.
  • Tissue diagnosis: sputum cytology; bronchoscopy with biopsy, brushings and washings; EBUS or CT-guided needle biopsy for peripheral or nodal lesions.
  • Histopathology with immunohistochemistry: p40/p63 (squamous), TTF-1 and napsin A (adenocarcinoma), chromogranin and synaptophysin (small cell).
  • Molecular tests in non-small cell carcinoma: EGFR, ALK, PD-L1.
  • Staging: PET-CT, MRI of the brain, bone scan as needed.
44a4a1b9a8:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: bronchogenic carcinoma (heavy smoker with cough, haemoptysis and weight loss; hoarseness suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement).

(ii) Diagnostic approach

  • Imaging: chest X-ray, then contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen for the tumour and staging.
  • Tissue diagnosis: sputum cytology; bronchoscopy with biopsy, brushings and washings; EBUS or CT-guided needle biopsy for peripheral or nodal lesions.
  • Histopathology with immunohistochemistry: p40/p63 (squamous), TTF-1 and napsin A (adenocarcinoma), chromogranin and synaptophysin (small cell).
  • Molecular tests in non-small cell carcinoma: EGFR, ALK, PD-L1.
  • Staging: PET-CT, MRI of the brain, bone scan as needed.
94c5f93a24:
Sialadenitis: inflammation of a salivary gland. Causes include viruses (mumps), bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, often with dehydration or duct obstruction), duct stones (sialolithiasis) and autoimmune disease (Sjogren syndrome).

Classification of salivary gland tumours

  • Benign epithelial: pleomorphic adenoma (the commonest), Warthin tumour, basal cell adenoma, oncocytoma, myoepithelioma.
  • Malignant epithelial: mucoepidermoid carcinoma (the commonest malignant), adenoid cystic carcinoma, acinic cell carcinoma, carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma, polymorphous adenocarcinoma, salivary duct carcinoma.
  • Non-epithelial: haemangioma, lymphangioma, lymphoma.
42fe448d62:
Gastritis: inflammation of the gastric mucosa.

Classification

  • Acute: NSAIDs, alcohol, severe stress (burns, shock), uraemia, chemotherapy, ischaemia.
  • Chronic: Helicobacter pylori gastritis (mainly antrum); autoimmune gastritis (body and fundus); others: chemical (reactive) gastropathy from bile reflux or NSAIDs, lymphocytic, eosinophilic and granulomatous gastritis.

Aetiopathogenesis of chronic gastritis

  • H. pylori: flagella and adhesins let it live in the mucus layer; urease makes ammonia that buffers acid and injures cells; CagA and VacA drive inflammation and cell damage.
  • Autoimmune: antibodies and T cells against parietal cells (the proton pump) and intrinsic factor destroy the oxyntic glands, causing achlorhydria, vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia) and high gastrin.

Morphology

  • Lymphocytes and plasma cells in the lamina propria; neutrophils in the glands when active.
  • Lymphoid follicles and curved bacilli in the surface mucus in H. pylori gastritis.
  • Gland loss (atrophy) and intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells, sometimes dysplasia.
  • Autoimmune type: diffuse atrophy of the body and fundus with neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia.
5d3af06250:
Peptic ulcer disease: a chronic breach of the lining that goes deeper than the muscularis mucosae, in parts of the gut bathed by acid and pepsin. Usual sites: the proximal duodenum (commonest) and the gastric antrum along the lesser curve; less often the distal oesophagus, a Meckel diverticulum or the jejunum in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Pathogenesis

An imbalance between damaging and protective forces.

  • Damaging: H. pylori infection (the commonest cause), NSAIDs (block prostaglandin synthesis), acid and pepsin, smoking, high gastrin (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome).
  • Protective: mucus and bicarbonate, tight junctions between epithelial cells, mucosal blood flow, prostaglandins, rapid epithelial renewal.
  • H. pylori raises acid output (fewer somatostatin cells, more gastrin), colonises gastric metaplasia in the duodenum and injures the mucosa with urease, toxins and the inflammation it provokes.

Diseases associated with H. pylori

  • Chronic (antral-predominant) gastritis.
  • Peptic ulcer, duodenal and gastric.
  • Gastric adenocarcinoma.
  • Gastric MALT lymphoma.
  • Associated with iron deficiency anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia.
b41133f835:
Diseases associated with H. pylori

  • Chronic (antral-predominant) gastritis.
  • Peptic ulcer, duodenal and gastric.
  • Gastric adenocarcinoma.
  • Gastric MALT lymphoma.
  • Associated with iron deficiency anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia.

Role of H. pylori in peptic ulcer

  • More acid: antral gastritis reduces somatostatin-producing D cells, so gastrin and acid output rise.
  • Duodenal colonisation: acid causes gastric metaplasia in the duodenum, which the organism then colonises, causing duodenitis and ulcer.
  • Direct injury: urease produces ammonia; proteases and phospholipases weaken the mucus layer; CagA and VacA damage epithelial cells and trigger IL-8 release.
  • Host inflammation: neutrophils and their reactive oxygen species add to mucosal damage.
  • Eradicating H. pylori heals ulcers and prevents them coming back.
4186e1bd1b:
• Distribution: Crohn disease can affect any part of the gut (most often the terminal ileum) with skip lesions; ulcerative colitis involves the rectum and spreads continuously upwards through the colon.
  • Depth: Crohn inflammation is transmural, causing fissures, fistulae and strictures; ulcerative colitis is limited to the mucosa and submucosa.
  • Granulomas: non-caseating granulomas are seen in Crohn disease, not in ulcerative colitis.
  • Also: cobblestone mucosa, creeping fat and perianal disease favour Crohn disease.
d619401442:
Two major pathways

  • APC / beta-catenin (chromosomal instability) pathway: the adenoma-carcinoma sequence; loss of APC, then KRAS activation, then loss of TP53 and SMAD4. About 80% of cases.
  • Microsatellite instability pathway: defective DNA mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2), as in Lynch syndrome, and the serrated pathway with BRAF mutation and gene hypermethylation.

Risk factors

  • Diet low in fibre and high in red and processed meat; obesity and inactivity.
  • Inflammatory bowel disease; adenomatous polyps; family history and hereditary syndromes (FAP, Lynch syndrome).
1d535923be:
• Non-neoplastic: hyperplastic polyp; inflammatory polyp (pseudopolyps of IBD); hamartomatous polyps (juvenile polyp, Peutz-Jeghers polyp); lymphoid polyp.
  • Neoplastic: adenomas (tubular, tubulovillous, villous); serrated lesions (sessile serrated lesion, traditional serrated adenoma).
  • Polyposis syndromes: familial adenomatous polyposis (with Gardner and Turcot variants), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis, Cowden syndrome.
  • In the stomach: fundic gland polyps, hyperplastic polyps, adenomas. Submucosal tumours (lipoma, GIST, neuroendocrine tumour) can also present as polyps.
e8be1bb5c2:
Classification of intestinal polyps

  • Non-neoplastic: hyperplastic polyp; inflammatory polyp (pseudopolyps of IBD); hamartomatous polyps (juvenile polyp, Peutz-Jeghers polyp); lymphoid polyp.
  • Neoplastic: adenomas (tubular, tubulovillous, villous); serrated lesions (sessile serrated lesion, traditional serrated adenoma).
  • Polyposis syndromes: familial adenomatous polyposis (with Gardner and Turcot variants), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis, Cowden syndrome.
  • In the stomach: fundic gland polyps, hyperplastic polyps, adenomas. Submucosal tumours (lipoma, GIST, neuroendocrine tumour) can also present as polyps.

Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome)

  • Autosomal dominant; a germline mutation in a DNA mismatch repair gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2), causing microsatellite instability.
  • Colorectal cancer at a young age, often right-sided, with few polyps (not polyposis); tumours are often mucinous with many tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes and have a better prognosis.
  • Other cancers: endometrium (the commonest), ovary, stomach, small bowel, urinary tract, hepatobiliary tract, brain and sebaceous skin tumours.
  • Diagnosis: Amsterdam criteria or Bethesda guidelines, tumour testing (MMR immunohistochemistry, MSI) and germline testing.
  • Management: colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years from age 20 to 25; screening for endometrial cancer.
8c1725d5a0:
(a) Most likely diagnosis: colorectal carcinoma, probably right-sided (caecum or ascending colon), which typically bleeds slowly and presents with iron deficiency anaemia in an older patient.

(b) Most important investigation: colonoscopy with biopsy for histopathological confirmation, followed by CT for staging and serum CEA as a baseline.
a5d258fc87:
Causes of hepatitis

  • Viral: hepatitis A, B, C, D and E; also EBV, CMV, herpes simplex, yellow fever.
  • Alcohol.
  • Drugs and toxins: paracetamol overdose, isoniazid, halothane, methotrexate.
  • Autoimmune hepatitis.
  • Metabolic: non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, Wilson disease, haemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
  • Other infections: leptospirosis, amoebiasis; ischaemic hepatitis in shock.

Outcomes of hepatitis B infection

  • Acute hepatitis with recovery: the usual course in adults (about 95%).
  • Subclinical infection with immunity.
  • Fulminant hepatitis with massive necrosis (under 1%).
  • Chronic hepatitis: about 5 to 10% of adults but up to 90% of infected newborns.
  • Carrier state without active disease.
  • Cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma after long-standing chronic infection.
  • Hepatitis D co-infection or superinfection worsens the course.
8034b25f60:
Gallstone: a solid concretion formed from bile constituents in the gallbladder or bile ducts: cholesterol, pigment (bilirubin) or mixed stones.

Complications

  • Gallbladder: biliary colic, acute and chronic cholecystitis, empyema, mucocele, gangrene and perforation.
  • Bile ducts: choledocholithiasis with obstructive jaundice, ascending cholangitis, Mirizzi syndrome.
  • Pancreas: acute pancreatitis.
  • Bowel: gallstone ileus through a cholecysto-enteric fistula.
  • Long term: carcinoma of the gallbladder.
094ce8e279:
(a) Most likely diagnosis: acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

  • Onset two weeks after a sore throat (the latent period of an immune reaction).
  • A nephritic picture: haematuria with RBC casts, proteinuria and periorbital oedema.
  • Low serum C3 (complement consumed); a raised ASO titre would support it further.

(b) Mechanism of renal injury

  • A nephritogenic strain of group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus infects the throat or skin.
  • Streptococcal antigens (such as SpeB) lodge in the glomeruli, or immune complexes form and deposit there: a type III (immune complex) reaction, seen as subepithelial humps on electron microscopy.
  • The deposits activate complement (mainly the alternative pathway), so serum C3 falls.
  • Neutrophils and monocytes are attracted, and endothelial and mesangial cells proliferate, narrowing the capillary lumens.
  • Filtration falls (oliguria, salt and water retention, oedema, hypertension), and damaged capillaries leak red cells (haematuria with RBC casts).
8feca0618c:
Chronic glomerulonephritis: the end stage of many glomerular diseases (RPGN, FSGS, membranous nephropathy, IgA nephropathy, MPGN), with progressive scarring and chronic kidney disease. The kidneys are small and finely granular, with hyalinised glomeruli, tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis and thickened arteries.

RPGN: pathogenesis

Severe glomerular injury tears the basement membrane; fibrin leaks into Bowman space and drives proliferation of parietal epithelial cells and influx of monocytes, forming crescents. Three immunological types:

  • Type I (anti-GBM): antibodies against the basement membrane, linear IgG; with lung haemorrhage in Goodpasture syndrome.
  • Type II (immune complex): granular deposits; after infection, in lupus nephritis, IgA nephropathy, Henoch-Schonlein purpura.
  • Type III (pauci-immune): little or no deposit; ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis).

RPGN: morphology

  • Gross: enlarged, pale kidneys with petechial haemorrhages.
  • Microscopy: crescents in most glomeruli (over 50%) compressing the tuft; fibrin within the crescents; later the crescents become fibrous and the glomeruli sclerose.
  • Immunofluorescence: linear, granular or negative, by type; electron microscopy shows breaks in the basement membrane.
0ef77fb8c7:
Pathogenesis of acute (post-streptococcal) glomerulonephritis

  • A nephritogenic strain of group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus infects the throat or skin.
  • Streptococcal antigens (such as SpeB) lodge in the glomeruli, or immune complexes form and deposit there: a type III (immune complex) reaction, seen as subepithelial humps on electron microscopy.
  • The deposits activate complement (mainly the alternative pathway), so serum C3 falls.
  • Neutrophils and monocytes are attracted, and endothelial and mesangial cells proliferate, narrowing the capillary lumens.
  • Filtration falls (oliguria, salt and water retention, oedema, hypertension), and damaged capillaries leak red cells (haematuria with RBC casts).

Classification of renal tumours

  • Benign: papillary adenoma, oncocytoma, angiomyolipoma, metanephric adenoma.
  • Malignant, adult: renal cell carcinoma (clear cell, papillary, chromophobe, collecting duct); urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis.
  • Malignant, childhood: Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma).
  • Others: sarcomas, lymphoma, metastases.
da00990709:
(a) Pyuria: an increased number of pus cells (neutrophils) in the urine, usually more than 5 per high-power field in centrifuged sediment. Pus cells without bacterial growth (sterile pyuria) suggest tuberculosis, stones, chlamydia or recent antibiotics.

(b) Laboratory approach to suspected UTI

  • Clean-catch midstream urine (or a catheter sample), examined promptly.
  • Dipstick: leukocyte esterase and nitrite.
  • Microscopy: pus cells, red cells, bacteria; white cell casts point to pyelonephritis.
  • Gram stain of the urine.
  • Culture and sensitivity: significant bacteriuria is usually 105 colony-forming units per mL or more (lower counts count in symptomatic or catheter samples).
  • Blood tests when unwell: complete blood count, CRP, urea and creatinine, blood culture.
  • Imaging (ultrasound of the urinary tract) for recurrent, complicated or male infections; urine for AFB in sterile pyuria.
1bed5c645c:
Risk factors for urothelial carcinoma

  • Cigarette smoking: the most important.
  • Occupational aromatic amines: aniline dye, rubber, leather and printing industries.
  • Also: Schistosoma haematobium infection (squamous type), cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiotherapy, analgesic (phenacetin) abuse.

Commonest presenting symptom: painless haematuria.
d7848497d1:
Histological types of renal cell carcinoma

  • Clear cell carcinoma: about 70 to 80%, linked to loss of the VHL gene.
  • Papillary carcinoma: about 10 to 15% (MET gene in the hereditary form).
  • Chromophobe carcinoma: about 5%, good prognosis.
  • Collecting duct (Bellini duct) carcinoma and renal medullary carcinoma: rare and aggressive.
  • Translocation-associated (Xp11) and unclassified carcinomas.

Most common: clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
78b5754ba1:
Painful swellings

  • Acute epididymo-orchitis (including mumps orchitis).
  • Torsion of the testis or of its appendage.
  • Trauma with haematocele.
  • Strangulated inguinal hernia.
  • Haemorrhage into a testicular tumour.

Painless swellings

  • Hydrocele and varicocele.
  • Epididymal cyst and spermatocele.
  • Testicular tumour (must be excluded).
  • Tuberculous epididymo-orchitis; syphilitic gumma.
  • Chronic haematocele; inguinal hernia.
44ac6ff5e9:
Causes of a raised serum PSA

  • Carcinoma of the prostate.
  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia.
  • Prostatitis.
  • Prostatic infarction, acute urinary retention.
  • Instrumentation: catheterisation, cystoscopy, prostatic biopsy, TURP; a vigorous rectal examination.
  • Recent ejaculation; increasing age.

Organ specific but not cancer specific

PSA is made almost only by prostatic epithelium, benign or malignant, so a raised level points to the prostate. But any condition that enlarges the gland or disturbs its epithelium (BPH, prostatitis, infarction, instrumentation) also raises it, and some cancers present with a normal value. Accuracy improves with PSA density, PSA velocity, the free-to-total ratio and age-specific ranges.
d293599879:
Diseases of the prostate

  • Inflammatory: acute bacterial prostatitis, chronic bacterial and non-bacterial prostatitis, granulomatous prostatitis.
  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia.
  • Neoplastic: prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia and adenocarcinoma.
  • Others: infarction, calculi.

Agents of epididymitis and orchitis

  • Non-specific: in young sexually active men, Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae; in older men and children, urinary pathogens such as E. coli and Pseudomonas; the mumps virus for orchitis.
  • Specific: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (starts in the epididymis); Treponema pallidum (starts in the testis, with gumma formation).
22dd029d11:
Benign prostatic hyperplasia: nodular hyperplasia of the glands and stroma of the prostate, arising in the transition (periurethral) zone of older men and driven by dihydrotestosterone.

Clinical manifestations

  • Obstructive: hesitancy, weak and intermittent stream, straining, terminal dribbling, a feeling of incomplete emptying.
  • Irritative: frequency, urgency, nocturia.
  • Complications: acute urinary retention, chronic retention with overflow, urinary infection, bladder stones and diverticula, haematuria, hydronephrosis and renal failure.
22be47b3d8:
(i) Probable diagnosis: carcinoma of the prostate with possible spinal (bone) metastasis, given the age, urinary symptoms, back pain and a palpable gland; benign prostatic hyperplasia is the main differential.

(ii) Serum marker: prostate-specific antigen (PSA), total and free; serum alkaline phosphatase helps if bone metastasis is suspected. Diagnosis is confirmed by prostatic biopsy.
bb81be69e5:
Premalignant lesion: cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), graded I to III (low- and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions).

Pathogenesis

  • Cause: persistent infection with high-risk HPV, mainly types 16 and 18, acquired sexually.
  • The virus infects immature basal cells at the transformation zone.
  • Viral DNA integrates into the host genome and the oncoproteins are over-expressed: E6 leads to degradation of p53 and activates telomerase; E7 binds RB, freeing E2F and driving the cell cycle.
  • Genomic instability builds up over years: low-grade lesion (CIN I), high-grade lesion (CIN II and III), then invasive carcinoma.
  • Cofactors: smoking, HIV and other immunosuppression, early sexual activity, multiple partners, high parity, long-term oral contraceptive use, other sexually transmitted infections.

Measures to reduce mortality

  • HPV vaccination of girls before sexual debut.
  • Regular screening (Pap smear, HPV DNA test or VIA) and treatment of CIN (cryotherapy, LEEP, cone biopsy).
  • Prompt investigation of abnormal bleeding or discharge, so cancer is diagnosed early.
  • Safer sexual practices, stopping smoking and public awareness.
b98ef4663a:
Histological types

  • Squamous cell carcinoma: about 75 to 80%.
  • Adenocarcinoma.
  • Adenosquamous carcinoma.
  • Neuroendocrine (small cell) carcinoma.

Aetiology and pathogenesis

  • Cause: persistent infection with high-risk HPV, mainly types 16 and 18, acquired sexually.
  • The virus infects immature basal cells at the transformation zone.
  • Viral DNA integrates into the host genome and the oncoproteins are over-expressed: E6 leads to degradation of p53 and activates telomerase; E7 binds RB, freeing E2F and driving the cell cycle.
  • Genomic instability builds up over years: low-grade lesion (CIN I), high-grade lesion (CIN II and III), then invasive carcinoma.
  • Cofactors: smoking, HIV and other immunosuppression, early sexual activity, multiple partners, high parity, long-term oral contraceptive use, other sexually transmitted infections.

Preventable? Yes. It has a long, detectable premalignant phase, a known viral cause and an effective vaccine.

Screening tests

  • Pap smear (conventional or liquid-based cytology).
  • HPV DNA testing, alone or with cytology.
  • VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid), widely used in Bangladesh.
  • Abnormal results lead to colposcopy and biopsy.
26cbd17d5e:
Likely diagnosis: invasive carcinoma of the cervix, most often squamous cell carcinoma.

Oncogenic virus: human papillomavirus, high-risk types 16 and 18.

Current measure: the HPV vaccine (bivalent, quadrivalent or nonavalent), together with screening for precancerous lesions.
1bb163bcf9:
(a) It suggests HPV infection with a squamous intraepithelial lesion (dysplasia). Koilocytes have a clear halo around an enlarged, dark, wrinkled nucleus, sometimes with two nuclei; a large dark nucleus with scant cytoplasm (high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio) points towards a high-grade lesion.

(b) Most common viral aetiology: human papillomavirus, especially high-risk type 16 (and 18); low-risk types 6 and 11 cause condylomas.
b22ee1c604:
Dysfunctional uterine bleeding: abnormal uterine bleeding with no structural or organic cause, due to a hormonal disturbance (most often anovulation). It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Causes by age group

  • Before puberty: precocious puberty, trauma, foreign body, vaginal tumour (sarcoma botryoides).
  • Adolescence: anovulatory cycles; bleeding disorders such as von Willebrand disease.
  • Reproductive age: complications of pregnancy (abortion, ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy); leiomyoma, adenomyosis, polyps; endometrial hyperplasia; thyroid disease; IUCD; anovulation.
  • Perimenopause: anovulatory cycles; polyps, fibroids, hyperplasia, carcinoma.
  • After menopause: endometrial atrophy, polyps, hyperplasia, endometrial carcinoma, exogenous oestrogen, cervical carcinoma.
35b6443d9f:
Causes of abnormal uterine bleeding (PALM-COEIN)

  • Structural: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy and hyperplasia.
  • Non-structural: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic (drugs, IUCD), Not yet classified.
  • Always exclude complications of pregnancy.

Common benign tumour of the uterus: leiomyoma (fibroid).

Complications of leiomyoma

  • Heavy menstrual bleeding and iron deficiency anaemia.
  • Pressure symptoms: urinary frequency or retention, constipation.
  • Infertility and recurrent miscarriage; in pregnancy, malpresentation, obstructed labour and postpartum haemorrhage.
  • Degeneration: hyaline, cystic, red (in pregnancy), fatty, calcification.
  • Torsion of a pedunculated fibroid; inversion of the uterus with a submucous fibroid; infection.
  • Malignant change (leiomyosarcoma) is very rare.
74e5eb4604:
Classification of uterine tumours

  • Endometrial epithelial: endometrial polyp; endometrial hyperplasia (without and with atypia); endometrial carcinoma (endometrioid type I; serous and clear cell type II); carcinosarcoma.
  • Mesenchymal: leiomyoma, smooth muscle tumour of uncertain malignant potential, leiomyosarcoma; endometrial stromal nodule and stromal sarcoma.
  • Mixed: adenomyoma, adenosarcoma.
  • Gestational trophoblastic disease.

Aetiology of endometrial carcinoma

  • Type I (endometrioid): unopposed oestrogen: obesity, nulliparity, early menarche and late menopause, anovulation and polycystic ovary syndrome, oestrogen-secreting ovarian tumours, oestrogen-only hormone therapy, tamoxifen; diabetes and hypertension; Lynch syndrome. Arises from atypical hyperplasia (PTEN, KRAS, mismatch repair defects).
  • Type II (serous): older women with atrophic endometrium; not oestrogen-driven; TP53 mutation.
dcde006db6:
Leiomyoma: a benign tumour of the smooth muscle of the myometrium (fibroid), the commonest tumour in women; it grows under oestrogen and shrinks after menopause.

Gross

  • Sharply circumscribed, firm, round grey-white nodules with a whorled cut surface; often multiple.
  • Intramural, submucosal or subserosal (sometimes pedunculated).
  • May show degeneration: hyaline, cystic, red (carneous) in pregnancy, calcification.

Microscopy

  • Interlacing bundles of uniform spindle smooth muscle cells with elongated, blunt-ended (cigar-shaped) nuclei and pink cytoplasm.
  • Little atypia, few mitoses and no tumour necrosis (which separates it from leiomyosarcoma).
a1f27fa127:
(a) Clinical diagnosis: ruptured ectopic (tubal) pregnancy with haemorrhagic shock: amenorrhoea, positive pregnancy test, an empty uterine cavity, abdominal pain and bleeding with hypotension and tachycardia.

(b) Classification of gestational trophoblastic disease

  • Molar pregnancies: complete mole (46,XX, all paternal), partial mole (triploid), and the locally invasive mole.
  • Trophoblastic neoplasms: gestational choriocarcinoma (highly malignant); PSTT, the placental site trophoblastic tumour; ETT, the epithelioid trophoblastic tumour.
  • Non-neoplastic lesions: an exaggerated placental site and the placental site nodule.
e8ef2e5498:
Risk factors

  • Female sex and increasing age.
  • Family history and inherited mutations: BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53, PTEN, PALB2, CHEK2.
  • Long oestrogen exposure: early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity or late first pregnancy, not breastfeeding, combined hormone therapy, obesity after menopause.
  • Alcohol; radiation to the chest; dense breasts; proliferative breast disease with atypia; previous breast cancer.

Prognostic factors

  • Major: in situ or invasive disease; distant metastasis; lymph node status; tumour size; locally advanced or inflammatory carcinoma.
  • Minor: histological type and grade; oestrogen and progesterone receptors; HER2; proliferation (Ki-67); molecular subtype; lymphovascular invasion.

Importance of identifying gene carriers

  • Earlier and closer surveillance (yearly MRI and mammography).
  • Risk-reducing surgery (mastectomy, salpingo-oophorectomy) or chemoprevention (tamoxifen).
  • Treatment choices: PARP inhibitors for BRCA-mutated cancers.
  • Screening for linked cancers (ovary, pancreas, prostate) and genetic counselling and testing of relatives.
615273a551:
(i) Most likely mutation: BRCA1 (BRCA2 is also possible): breast cancer at a young age in the patient and her mother, with ovarian cancer in her sister.

(ii) Normal function: BRCA1 is a tumour suppressor that repairs double-strand DNA breaks by homologous recombination, keeping the genome stable and supporting cell-cycle checkpoints. Losing both copies lets mutations accumulate.
23afd05ad2:
Types of thyroiditis

  • Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic lymphocytic).
  • Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis.
  • Subacute lymphocytic (painless and postpartum) thyroiditis.
  • Riedel thyroiditis (fibrosing, IgG4-related).
  • Acute infective (suppurative) thyroiditis.
  • Drug-induced (amiodarone, interferon) and radiation thyroiditis.

Clinical features of Hashimoto thyroiditis

  • Middle-aged women most often.
  • Painless, diffuse, firm (rubbery) goitre.
  • Gradual hypothyroidism: tiredness, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, menstrual upset.
  • Sometimes a brief early thyrotoxic phase (hashitoxicosis).
  • Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies; associated autoimmune diseases (type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia).
  • Raised risk of B-cell (MALT) lymphoma of the thyroid.
871279ad8b:
• Graves disease: an autoimmune disease. Antibodies against the TSH receptor (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins) switch the gland on, causing diffuse hyperplasia and hyperthyroidism. Linked to genes (HLA-DR3, CTLA4), female sex, and triggers such as stress, infection and iodine.
  • Diffuse non-toxic (simple) goitre: impaired thyroid hormone synthesis raises TSH, which enlarges the gland while the patient stays euthyroid. Causes: iodine deficiency (endemic goitre), dietary goitrogens and drugs (lithium), higher demand in puberty and pregnancy, inherited defects of hormone synthesis.
195e519683:
Premalignant lesions of skin

  • Actinic (solar) keratosis.
  • Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) and arsenical keratosis.
  • Xeroderma pigmentosum.
  • Dysplastic naevi and giant congenital naevi.
  • Chronic scars, burns and ulcers (Marjolin ulcer); radiation dermatitis.
  • Leukoplakia and erythroplakia of mucosa.

Malignant melanoma

  • A malignant tumour of melanocytes, arising in the skin and less often the eye, mucosa or acral sites (soles, nail beds).
  • Risk factors: UV exposure (especially sunburn), fair skin, many or dysplastic naevi, family history (CDKN2A), xeroderma pigmentosum.
  • Warning signs (ABCDE): Asymmetry, irregular Border, varied Colour, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolution (change); bleeding or ulceration.
  • Types: superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, acral lentiginous.
  • Growth: a radial phase, then a vertical phase that can metastasise.
  • Microscopy: atypical melanocytes with large nuclei and prominent red nucleoli, spreading upwards in the epidermis and invading the dermis; S-100, HMB-45, Melan-A and SOX10 are positive.
  • Prognosis: Breslow thickness (the most important), ulceration, mitoses and node status; spreads to lymph nodes, lung, liver and brain.
e5ff3800ea:
Bullous diseases of skin

  • Pemphigus (vulgaris, foliaceus): blisters within the epidermis, antibodies to desmogleins.
  • Bullous pemphigoid: blisters below the epidermis, antibodies to hemidesmosome proteins.
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis: IgA deposits, linked to coeliac disease.
  • Linear IgA disease, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, pemphigoid gestationis.
  • Inherited: epidermolysis bullosa.
  • Other blistering conditions: burns, bullous impetigo, porphyria cutanea tarda, and the drug-related spectrum of erythema multiforme through to toxic epidermal necrolysis.

Premalignant lesions of skin

  • Actinic (solar) keratosis.
  • Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) and arsenical keratosis.
  • Xeroderma pigmentosum.
  • Dysplastic naevi and giant congenital naevi.
  • Chronic scars, burns and ulcers (Marjolin ulcer); radiation dermatitis.
  • Leukoplakia and erythroplakia of mucosa.
f9d42a74f1:
(i) Differential diagnosis

  • Acral lentiginous malignant melanoma: the most likely (rapidly growing pigmented ulcer on the toe of an older man).
  • Pigmented squamous or basal cell carcinoma.
  • Kaposi sarcoma.
  • Subungual haematoma; pyogenic granuloma; a diabetic foot ulcer with pigmentation.

(ii) Confirmation

  • Dermoscopy, then an excision (full-thickness) biopsy with histopathology; avoid shave biopsy or FNAC of the primary.
  • Immunohistochemistry: S-100, HMB-45, Melan-A, SOX10.
  • Staging: Breslow thickness and ulceration, sentinel lymph node biopsy, imaging for distant spread; BRAF testing for treatment.
